--- Transcript ---
00:00 Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. uh quick intros? i'm jordan from redwood, ae. lina, maya on my team.
00:08 Marcus: hey Marcus here, CTO at Archimedes. we run inference for a couple of trading signals, also internal research.
00:13 Sofia: Sofia, head of ML ops, dealing with infra and cost.
00:16 Rahul: Rahul, infra lead, mostly kubernetes networking and security.
00:20 Jordan: awesome. goal for today is to learn about your workloads and constraints, particularly around per-token economics and where hosted vs dedicated vs private fit. we'll try to be concrete.
00:29 Marcus: perfect. high level: we use LLMs for alt data enrichment and some real-time summarization of news. latency matters for a subset, but a lot is batch. monthly budget is roughly $15k for inference. want to see if we can get predictable unit cost and a path to scale.
00:45 Lina: got it. when you say batch vs real time, can you quantify percent?
00:48 Marcus: roughly 70% batch (nightly runs), 30% low-latency requests under 200ms p95 for the trading alerts. token distribution is heavy on short prompts — 20-80 tokens typically, but sometimes long context up to 1.5k for some workflows.
01:05 Jordan: helpful. key levers we'll talk through: per-token pricing on hosted, reserved capacity for dedicated, and private for VPC/on-prem for compliance. plus batching and prefix/KV caching which affects effective unit cost.
01:16 Sofia: also curious about data retention, audit logs, KMS integration — we have strict encryption requirements.
01:21 Lina: we support KMS/HSM integrations, SOC 2, SSO/SAML, and audit logs in the console. we can share the security whitepaper after.
01:30 Rahul: okay thanks. on cost — how does hosted per-token pricing change with batching? like, if we batch a lot, do we see linear reductions?
01:36 Lina: good question. raw per-token price on hosted is a baseline. with batching, effective tokens per GPU second improves so your cost per output token goes down. it's not strictly linear because of latency SLOs and memory constraints — but for your nightly jobs where latency doesn't matter, you can often get 2-4x improvement in unit cost vs single-request inference.
01:55 Jordan: also prefix/KV caching can cut cost for repeated prompts — if many requests share a large prompt prefix, caching the KV cache avoids recomputing tokens for the prefix, so you only pay for new tokens. for your 70% batch workloads it could be a big lever.
02:10 Marcus: that sounds promising. can you give an example? say we have 1M requests/month, avg 50 tokens, but 80% share a 40-token prefix — what does that look like?
02:20 Lina: simple back-of-envelope: if 80% share a 40-token prefix you avoid recomputing those 40 tokens each time — so you may only pay for the 10 new tokens for those requests. multiply out and your effective tokens processed drops significantly — we'd run the exact math in the pricing worksheet.
02:33 Sofia: for dedicated/reserved capacity, what's the commitment model — monthly/annual? and how much predictability vs hosted?
02:40 Jordan: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools with monthly or annual commits. it's priced more like reserved instances so your unit cost drops with commitment. predictability is much higher: you get guaranteed throughput and capacity isolation, which is useful for latency-sensitive pipelines. Hosted is pay-as-you-go and simpler to start.
02:54 Rahul: if we go dedicated, does Redwood manage autoscaling or do we manage the fleet?
02:58 Lina: Redwood manages the runtime, autoscaling policies can be configured, and you can set burst/baseline thresholds. for Private (VPC/on-prem) customers, you run the control plane in your environment and we provide the runtime — ops models vary.
03:11 Marcus: what's typical per-token numbers? i know it varies by model size and quantization.
03:16 Lina: yes a lot depends on model, quantization, and kernel efficiency. for example, an Llama-2-13B quantized might produce X cost baseline on hosted — i'll avoid quoting exact public numbers on a call but we'll put model-level benchmarks in the worksheet. important point: quantized models and int8 runtimes can reduce cost 2-3x at small quality tradeoffs.
03:36 Marcus: okay quality tradeoffs are fine for some workloads. for signals we need higher quality. can we run mixed-routing — critical ops on dedicated, batch on hosted?
03:44 Jordan: absolutely. Smart routing lets you send high-priority low-latency traffic to dedicated or a higher-tier instance and route batch to cheaper pooled hosted capacity. we can set fallback policies too.
03:54 Sofia: about pilot — we want to run a 1-week pilot, run our nightly batch and a subset of low-latency requests. what data/traces do you need?
04:02 Lina: request traces with timestamps, token counts, sequence length distribution, and concurrency targets. also security constraints around the traces — if they contain PII we can do an NDA or accept sanitized traces.
04:12 Marcus: we'll sanitize and share. one more: how do you handle caching across user sessions? our prompts sometimes vary slightly, will caching still help?
04:20 Lina: caching is prefix-based; small variations in later tokens still benefit if the prefix matches. we also do approximate caching for fuzzy matches but that's more advanced.
04:29 Rahul: are there any gotchas for CPU vs GPU memory on dedicated? certain quantization needs more CPU ops, right?
04:35 Lina: good callout. quantized int8 tends to be GPU-memory friendly but requires optimized kernels; some extreme quant formats need CPU fallback which impacts latency. we'll capture those tradeoffs in the recommendation sheet per workload.
04:47 Marcus: security checklist — SSO, logs, retention, and data residency. we operate in EU and US. can Private be deployed in our VPC with customer KMS?
04:56 Jordan: yes Private supports VPC and on-prem with customer-managed KMS and full audit logs. we'll include deployment options and compliance artifacts in the follow-up.
05:04 Sofia: fine. about pricing model — any minimums for Dedicated?
05:08 Jordan: Dedicated has sizing minimums because it's reserved GPU capacity. typically customers commit to a baseline throughput; we'll propose a few tiers based on your traces.
05:16 Marcus: our budget is a hard cap at $15k/mo for inference. if Dedicated requires higher commit, we'd need to show that unit economics offset the commit.
05:24 Lina: we can model hosted vs dedicated with your actual traces in the worksheet: show expected monthly spend, tokens saved from caching, and potential savings from quantization and batching.
05:33 Rahul: one technical question: for batching, how do you control max latency for 200ms p95? is there adaptive batching?
05:40 Lina: yes adaptive batching — the runtime will prioritize latency SLOs and dynamically adjust batch sizes and time windows. you can pin a route to a lower-latency node pool to keep p95 under target; batching then operates within those constraints.
05:51 Marcus: sounds good. can you also instrument per-route cost in the console so product folks can see which flows cost most?
05:58 Maya: yep console has token-level cost breakdowns per route/model and tracing hooks. we can enable a demo view for you.
06:05 Sofia: about SLAs — what's uptime for Dedicated?
06:09 Jordan: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets, we'll include SLAs in the contract appendix.
06:13 Marcus: any educational material on how to design prompts to maximize cache hits?
06:18 Lina: yes we have a best-practices doc — standardize prefixes, minimize irrelevant context, reuse system prompts — we'll share that.
06:25 Marcus: great. i'm concerned about unpredictable token spikes from long contexts. how do you protect against cost overruns?
06:31 Jordan: you can set per-route quotas and alerting. also routing policies can fallback to smaller model variants if cost thresholds hit. and you can set hard caps to reject requests above configured token limits.
06:43 Rahul: for the benchmarking pilot, what do we need to provide?
06:46 Lina: sample traces, a small dataset to run end-to-end latency and quality checks, and acceptance criteria for quality (e.g., BLEU/ROUGE or human eval). we'll run both hosted and dedicated configs and show per-token cost.
06:58 Marcus: timeline?
07:00 Jordan: we'll send pricing worksheet and pilot plan within 3 business days. then schedule SE deep-dive to scope benchmarks. pilot could start within 2 weeks of trace handoff.
07:10 Sofia: okay. any compliance caveats for private/on-prem?
07:13 Maya: for on-prem, our control plane can run in your environment; you'll manage network and KMS; there is an integration checklist and support options.
07:22 Marcus: competitors — we've looked at Anthropic and Bedrock; main things we like about Redwood are batching/kv caching and a unified experience across hosted/dedicated/private. will want to validate latency claims.
07:33 Jordan: understood. we'll include benchmark evidence and an architecture note showing kernel optimizations we use.
07:39 Rahul: small nit: will we be able to use our existing prometheus stack?
07:43 Lina: yes we expose metrics and traces; you can integrate with Prometheus and your tracing system.
07:48 Marcus: ok let's wrap with explicit next steps.
07:50 Jordan: recap: Jordan will send pricing worksheet and cost model (3 days), Lina will schedule the benchmarking deep-dive and detail pilot requirements, Marcus will share sanitized traces and token distribution (by end of week). action items in the notes.
07:59 Sofia: good. thanks everyone.
08:01 Marcus: thanks, talk soon.
